item.title: UK to offer Saudi Arabia aerial refueling to counter Houthi attacks
item.description:
Saudi authorities issued a new alert over attacks from Yemen, where fighting intensified, as fears grew of the Middle East conflict expanding. Saudi Arabia warned residents in a province bordering Yemen of potential danger after Iran-backed Houthi fighters made lightning advances on their side of the border ; days earlier, Riyadh itself was hit by a Houthi attack. Britain and France offered support for Saudi military efforts and energy infrastructure respectively, but the US, the Middle East’s military giant, has so far opted against backing Riyadh’s campaign against the Houthis, The New York Times reported. Instead, Washington has proposed a multibillion dollar fund to rebuild energy facilities across the Gulf , according to The Wall Street Journal. — Prashant Rao

Covered by 1 billionaire/family, 1 nonprofit, 1 public.
Sources: France 24, Semafor, The Guardian

item.title: Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights
item.description:
Thousands flee fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces Middle East live – latest updates As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence. Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict. Continue reading...

Sources: BBC News, The Guardian

item.description:

Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility, Los Angeles county medical examiner records show. item.title: Today in Supreme Court History: September 22, 2005
item.description:
Source image: Bryan Dozier/NurPhoto via AP The Supreme Court continues to make consequential rulings in the shadows. I analyzed tens of thousands of case files from the court’s online archives , parsing through filings to separate simple requests for deadline extensions from challenges to long-established constitutional rights. I discovered that in the term that ended in 2025, the justices issued more substantive decisions on their emergency docket than in cases argued in open court. Experts told me this was likely the first time this has happened in the court’s modern history. Representatives from the Supreme Court did not respond to my questions. Since I reported that story in July, more major rulings have been made on the emergency docket, often called the “shadow docket,” where justices rarely hear arguments and often issue unsigned orders that don’t explain how they arrived at…

Covered by 2 nonprofit.
Sources: ProPublica, Reason

item.title: Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan
item.description:
Rescuers search for missing in collapsed homes after storm causes landslides, travel chaos and power outages Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least four people and injured 22 in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday. Dujuan – which brought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph) – was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings. Continue reading...

item.title: British Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shooting
item.description:
Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to plan the massacre. The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence. Continue reading...
